questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question:
With initial condition x(1) = 0.5, the solution of the differential equation,
\(t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t\) is
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation is \(t \frac{d x}{d t}+x=t\) with initial condition \(x(1)=\frac{1}{2}\) which is same as \(\frac{d x}{d t}+\frac{x}{t}=1\)
Which is a linear differential equation
\(\frac{d x}{d t}+P x=Q\)
Where, \(P=\frac{1}{t}\) and Q=1
Integrating factor \(=e^{\int P t t=e^{1 \frac{1}{t} d t}}\)
\(=e^{\log _{e} t}=t\)
Solution is
\[\begin{aligned} x \cdot(I F)&=\int Q \cdot(I F) d t+C \\ x \cdot t&=\int 1 \cdot t \cdot d t+C \\ x t&=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C \\ x&=\frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t} \\ \text{Put},x(1)=\frac{1}{2}&\\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow\quad C&=0 \\ \text{So, }\left[x=\frac{t}{2}\right]& \text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}\]

questions.question:
The radiation pattern of an antenna in spherical co-ordinates is given by
\(F(\theta )=cos^{4}\theta ;0\leq \theta\leq \pi /2\)
The directivity of the antenna is
questions.explanation:
\(F(\theta)=\cos ^{4} \theta, 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi / 2\)
we know that directivity D is
\(D=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\pi_{\mathrm{rad}}} \qquad\ldots(1)\)
\(\mathrm{F}(\theta)\) is nothing but radiation intensity \(u(\theta, \phi)\) and
\(W_{\mathrm{rad}}\) is radiated power.
\(W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \phi\qquad\ldots(2)\)
above equation is written from the formula
\(W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\iint_{\theta \phi} u(\theta, \phi) d \Omega\)
where \(\alpha \Omega\) is solid angle and \(d \Omega=\sin \theta d \theta d \phi\)
So from (2)
\[\begin{aligned} W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin d \theta d \phi \\ W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=2 \pi \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \theta \\W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=-2 \pi\left[\frac{\cos ^{5} \theta}{5}\right]_{0}^{\pi / 2}\\ W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=\frac{2 \pi}{5}&\ldots(3)\\ \text { So, } \quad D&=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{5}\right)}=10 u_{\max }=10\\ &\text { In } \mathrm{dB} \text { directivity }=10 \mathrm{log}_{10} \mathrm{D}=10 \mathrm{dB}\end{aligned}\]

questions.question:
A system with transfer function
\(G(s)=\frac{(s^{2}+9)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)}\)
is excited by sin(\(\omega\) t). The steady-state output of the system is zero at
questions.explanation:
Transfer function is
\[\begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \\ \text{Input }\quad X(s)&=L \cdot T[\sin \omega t]\\ X(s)&=\frac{\omega}{s^{2}+\omega^{2}} \end{aligned}\]
So output
\(Y(s)=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}\)
Now
\(\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} y(t)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} S Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}\)
this will be zero if \(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\) will cancel \(\left(s^{2}+9\right)\) term as only then final value theorem will be applicable.
So at \(\omega^{2}=9 \Rightarrow \omega=3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec},\) steady state output will be zero.

questions.question: Given \(f(z)=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3}\). If C is a counterclockwise path in the z-plane such that |z+1|=1, the value of \(\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint_{C}f(z)dz\) is
questions.explanation:
Given,
\[\begin{aligned} f(z) &=\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+3} \\ &=\frac{(z+3)-2(z+1)}{(z+1)(z+3)} \\ &=\frac{-z+1}{(z+1)(z+3)} \end{aligned}\]
Poles are at -1 and -3 i.e. (-1,0) and (-3,0)
From figure below of |z+1|=1
we see that (-1,0) is inside the circle and (-3,0) is outside the circle.


Residue theorem says,
\(\frac{1}{2 \pi j} \oint_{C} f(z) d z=\) Residue of those poles which are inside C .
So, the required integral \(\frac{1}{2 \pi j} \oint_{C} f(z) d z\) is given by the residue of function at pole (-1,0) (which is inside the circle).
This residue is \(=\frac{-(-1)+1}{(-1+3)}=\frac{2}{2}=1\)

\[\begin{aligned} y&=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau) \cos (3 \tau) d \tau \\ y\left(t-t_{0}\right)&=\int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} x(\tau) \cos (3 \tau) d \tau \\ y^{\prime}(t) \text { for input } &x\left(t-t_{0}\right) \text { , is }\\ y^{\prime}(t)&=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x\left(\tau-t_{0}\right) \cos 3 \tau d \tau \\ y^{\prime}(t)&=\int_{-\infty}^{\left(t-t_{0}\right)} x(\tau) \cos 3\left(\tau+t_{0}\right) d \tau \end{aligned}\]
\(y^{\prime}(t) \neq y\left(t-t_{0}\right)\)

So, K=2

Consider the differential equation \(\frac{d^{2}y(t)}{dt^{2}}+2\frac{dy(t)}{dt}+y(t)=\delta (t)\) with \(y(t)|_{t=0^{-}}=-2\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt}|_{t=0^{-}}=0\)
The numerical value of \(\frac{dy}{dt}|_{t=0^{+}}\) is
questions.explanation:
\(\frac{d^{2} y}{d t^{2}}+2 \frac{d y}{d t}+y(t)=8(t)\)
taking Laplace transform on both the sides we
have
\[\begin{array}{l} \left[s^{2} Y(s)-s y\left(0^{-}\right)-y^{\prime}(0)\right]+2\left[Y(s)-y\left(0^{-}\right)\right]+Y(s)=1\\ s^{2} Y(s)+2 s+2 s Y(s)+4+\eta(s)=1 \\ \left(s^{2}+2 s+1\right) Y(s)=-(2 s+3) \\ Y(s)=\frac{-(2 s+3)}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ Y(s)=-\left[\frac{2}{(s+1)}+\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad Y(t)=-\left[2 e^{-t}+t e^{-7}\right] u(t) \\ \frac{d y}{d t}=-\left[-2 e^{-t}+e^{-t}-t e^{-1}\right] u(t) \\ \left.\frac{d y}{d t}\right|_{\mathrm{at} t=0^{+}}=-[-2+1-0] \\ \left.\frac{d y}{d t}\right|_{\mathrm{at} t=0^{+}}=1 \end{array}\]

X is such that P(X=0) = 9/10, then the probability of error for an optimum receiver will be
questions.explanation:
\[\begin{array}{l} P\left(y_{0} \mid x_{0}\right) P\left(x_{0}\right)=\frac{7}{8} \times \frac{9}{10}=\frac{63}{80} \\ P\left(y_{0} \mid x_{1}\right) P\left(x_{1}\right)=\frac{1}{8} \times \frac{1}{10}=\frac{1}{80} \\ P\left(y_{1} \mid x_{0}\right) P\left(x_{0}\right)=\frac{1}{8} \times \frac{9}{10}=\frac{9}{80} \\ P\left(y_{1} \mid x_{1}\right) P\left(x_{1}\right)=\frac{7}{8} \times \frac{1}{10}=\frac{7}{80} \end{array}\]
\(P\left(y_{0} \mid x_{0}\right) P\left(x_{0}\right)>P\left(y_{0} \mid x_{1}\right) P\left(x_{1}\right);\) So, when a
symbol is received as \(y_{0}\) , the decision can be
made in favour of \(x_{0}\) in an optimum way.
\(P\left(y, \mid x_{0}\right) P\left(x_{0}\right)>P\left(y_{1} \mid x_{1}\right) P\left(x_{1}\right) ;\) So, when a
symbol is received as \(y_{1}\), the decision can be
made in favour of \(x_{0}\) in an optimum way.
So, for the given BSC, with optimum receiver, both
the received symbols will be decoded as \(x_{0}\)
Hence, the probability of error is equal to the
probability of transmitting \(x_{1}\)
So, \(P_{e}=P\left(x_{1}\right)=1 / 10\)

questions.explanation:
For phase modulator
\(\phi(t)=2 \pi f_{c} t+k_{p} m(t)\)
maximum phase deviation is
\(\left(\phi_{D}\right)_{\max }=k_{p} \max [m(t)]=2 k_{p} \quad\ldots(1)\)
for frequency modulator
\[\begin{aligned} \phi(t) &=2 \pi f_{c} t+2 \pi k_{f} \int_{0}^{t} m(t) d t \\ \left(\phi_{D}^{\prime}\right)_{\max } &=2 \pi k_{t} t\left[\int_{0}^{t} m(t) d t\right]_{\max } \\ \left(\phi_{D}^{\prime}\right)_{\max } &=2 \pi k_{t}\left[\int_{0}^{2} m(t) d t\right] \\ \left(\phi_{D}^{\prime}\right)_{\max } &=2 \pi k_{f}\left[\int_{0}^{2} 2 d t\right] \\ \left(\phi_{D}^{\prime}\right)_{\max } &=8 \pi k_{f} &\ldots(2)\\ \text{given}\\ \left(\phi_{D}^{\prime}\right)_{\max }&=\left(\phi_{D}\right)_{\max }\\ 8 \pi k_{f}&=2 k_{p} \\ \mid \frac{k_{p}}{k_{f}}&=4 \pi \end{aligned}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: The maximum value of \(f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5\) in the interval [1, 6] is
questions.explanation:
We need absolute maximum of
\(f(x)=x^{3}-9 x^{2}+24 x+5\) in the interval [1,6]
First find local maximum if any by putting \(f^{\prime}(x)=0\)
\[\begin{aligned} \text{i.e.}\quad f^{\prime}(x)&=3 x^{2}-18 x+24=0\\ \text{i.e.}\quad x^{2}-6 x+8&=0 \\ x &=2,4 \\ \text { Now } \quad f^{\prime \prime}(x) &=6 x-18 \\ f^{\prime \prime}(2) &=12-18=-6 \lt 0\\ &\text{(So x=2 is a point of local maximum)}\\ \text{ and }f^{\prime \prime}(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ &\text{(So x=4 is a point of local minimum)} \end{aligned}\]
Now tabulate the values of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below:
\[\begin{array}{l|l} x & f(x) \\ 1 & 21 \\ 2 & 25 \\ 6 & 41 \end{array}\]
Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.

questions.question: Given that \[A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2&0 \end{bmatrix}\] and \[I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}\], the value of \(A^{3}\) is
questions.explanation:
\[A=\left[\begin{array}{rr}-5 & -3 \\ 2 & 0\end{array}\right] \text{ and } I=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\]
Characteristic equation of A is
\[\begin{aligned} \left|\begin{array}{rr}-5-\lambda & -3 \\ 2 & 0-\lambda\end{array}\right|&=0\\ (-5-\lambda)(-\lambda)+6&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}+5 \lambda+6&=0 \\ \text{ So,}\quad A^{2}+5 A+6 I&=0 \\ &\text{(by Cayley Hamilton theorem) }\\ \Rightarrow \quad A^{2}=-5 A-6 I& \end{aligned}\]
Multiplying by A on both sides, we have,
\[\begin{aligned} A^{3} &=-5 A^{2}-6 A \\ \Rightarrow \quad A^{3} &=-5(-5 A-6 I)-6 A \\ &=19 A+30I \end{aligned}\]

questions.question:
With 10 V dc connected at port A in the linear nonreciprocal two-port network shown below, the following were observed:
(i) 1\(\Omega\) connected at port B draws a current of 3 A
(ii) 2.5 \(\Omega\) connected at port B draws a current of 2 A

For the same network, with 6 V dc connected at port A, 1 \(\Omega\) connected at port B draws 7/3 A. If 8 V dc is connected to port A, the open circuit voltage at port B is
questions.explanation:
Case (i):
\[\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=10 \mathrm{V}, R_{L}=1 \Omega, I=3 \mathrm{A} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=I\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+R_{L}\right)=3\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+1\right)\\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=3 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+3 &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}\]
Case (ii):
\[\begin{aligned} R_{L}&=2.5 \Omega, I=2 \mathrm{A}, V_{\mathrm{DC}}=10 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+2.5\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+5 &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}\]
From equations (i) and (ii)
\(V_{\mathrm{Th}}=9 \mathrm{V} and R_{\mathrm{TH}}=2 \Omega \quad\ldots(iii)\)
Now, \(V_{Th}\) depends on independent voltage source and varies with applied voltage. \(R_{Th}\) does not depend on voltage source and is same for any applied voltage source, since voltage_ source is short circuited while calculating \(R_{Th}\)
\[\begin{aligned} \text{For }V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=6 \mathrm{V}, R_{\mathrm{L}}=1 \Omega, I=7 / 3 \\ V_{T h}&=I\left(R_{T h}+R_{L}\right) \\ V_{T h}&=\frac{7}{3}(2+1)=7 V &\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}\]
\(\because\)The network is linear and non reciprocal, it may
contain dependent voltage source
\[\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad V_{T h}&=a V+b \\ \Rightarrow \quad 9&=a 10+b \quad \text{from equation (iii)} \\ \text{and }\quad 7&=a 6+b \quad\text{from equation (iv)} \\ \end{aligned}\]
Solving, we get a=1/2 and b=4
\(\therefore \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}=\frac{V}{2}+4=\frac{8}{2}+4=8 \mathrm{V}\)

questions.subject: electromagnetics
questions.question:
An infinitely long uniform solid wire of radius a carries a uniform dc current of density \(\overrightarrow{j}\).

The magnetic field at a distance \(r\) from the center of the wire is proportional to
options: \(r \; for \; r \lt a \; and \; 1/r^{2}\; for \;r \gt a\)
\(0 \; for \; r  \lt  a \; and \; 1 /r \; for \; r  \gt  a\)
\(r \; for \; r  \lt  a \; and \; 1 /r \; for \; r  \gt  a\)
\(0 \; for\; r \lt a \; and \; 1/r^{2} \;for \; r \gt a\)
questions.explanation:
We know that magnetic flux density at a distance r from the wire is,
\[\begin{aligned} |B| &=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r} \\ \text { For } r \lt a \rightarrow I&=J \cdot \pi r^{2} \\ \text { so } \quad |B|&=\frac{\mu_{0} J r}{2}\\ |B| \propto r \text { for } r \lt a \\ \text { for } r \gt a,\quad I&=J \times \pi a^{2} \\ \text { So, } |B|&=\frac{\mu_{0} J \pi a^{2}}{2 \pi r} \\ |B| \propto \frac{1}{r} \text { for } r \gt a \end{aligned}\]
